summary:
Irkutsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, and the sources document no oblast-level deviation from it. Same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and no specific legal protections exist for transgender people.

Legal gender recognition was abolished in 2023, when Vladimir Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and gender changes on official documents. The Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that includes, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition.

Penalties under that framework are severe. The propaganda statute carries administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to four years in prison; participation in the designated extremist movement carries two to six years and organising it six to ten years, and Human Rights Watch reports that participants face up to twelve years.

Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers; official national government warnings tell LGBT travellers the same.

Gender-affirming care cannot be obtained lawfully anywhere in the country. Survey data cited by the UK Home Office place the Siberian Federal District, which includes Irkutsk Oblast, at 24% for discrimination by healthcare providers who knew a patient's sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was recorded by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times described arrests, club raids and extremism charges as the defining conditions of LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, reporting on 23 June 2025 a St Petersburg queer woman who called herself "a second-class citizen" after the designation.

In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Human Rights Watch, on 30 June 2025, called on governments to offer safe haven to people fleeing Russia.
localsOnly:
Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions. Human Rights Watch counted 101 extremism convictions tied to the 2023 Supreme Court designation as of 30 June 2025, and recorded that between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, one of whom died by suicide in pretrial detention and two of whom were sentenced to prison; a further 81 people in 98 cases were found guilty under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols.

Residents of the Siberian Federal District report worse conditions than the country overall. The same survey data place the district at 24% for discrimination by healthcare providers who knew a patient's sexual orientation or gender identity, and show Siberian respondents to be more closeted than the whole-study sample.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented in the wider Siberian area. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports enforcement, prosecutions or police conduct recorded specifically in Irkutsk Oblast. The oblast-level position is therefore inferred from the national framework and from Siberian Federal District survey data rather than from local records.

Whether conversion-therapy practice of the kind documented near Novosibirsk occurs in Irkutsk Oblast is unresolved; the case cited is from elsewhere in Siberia and is presented as an illustration of regional risk, not as an Irkutsk finding.

No source addresses document or gender-marker screening at border control or at Irkutsk airport, nor the treatment of transgender travellers' passports during entry checks. That question is not sourced here.

No source addresses local access to facilities, name-change procedure at the oblast registry level, or oblast-level hate-crime charging practice. The national bans on legal gender change and gender-affirming care are stated as the operative rule, with no local exception documented.
